title: Cyclic groups and order
objectives: Find the order of an element and the generators of a cyclic group.

screens.title: Walking round six seats
screens.prose: Six seats $0, 1, \dots, 5$ sit round a table, the residues of $\mathbb{Z}_6$. Each arrow adds the step modulo 6. Switch the step from 1 to 5, then to 2.
screens.question: With steps of 2, how many seats does a walk from 0 visit, counting 0?

hints.text: Follow the arrows from 0 with the step set to 2.
From 0: 2, then 4, then back to 0.
The walk visits 0, 2 and 4 only.

feedback.correct: Right: 0, 2, 4. Steps of 2 split the seats into two triangles.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow the arrows from 0 until you return.

byKey.all: You counted every seat. Steps of 2 never reach the odd seats from 0.
byKey.two: You left out seat 0. The walk from 0 visits 0, 2 and 4.

explain.text: Steps of 1 or 5 visit all six seats. Steps of 2 visit only $\{0, 2, 4\}$ from 0, and $\{1, 3, 5\}$ from 1.

screens.title: Powers on the circle
screens.prose: The 12th roots of unity are $\zeta^j$ for $j = 0, \dots, 11$, with $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/12}$. Here $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ (`complex` l4-roots-of-unity), and turns add (`trig` l12). The map $z \mapsto z^k$ sends $\zeta^j$ to $\zeta^{jk}$.
screens.question: Set k to 4. On how many different points do the twelve images land?

hints.text: Watch the w-plane as k moves to 4.
$\zeta^{4j}$ is a turn by $4j$ twelfths, and $4j$ modulo 12 is 0, 4 or 8.
The images are $\zeta^0, \zeta^4, \zeta^8$: three points, the cube roots of unity.

feedback.correct: Right: three points. Each is hit four times.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the distinct dots in the w-plane at k = 4.

byKey.twelve: You counted the twelve inputs. At k = 4 they pile up on three outputs.
byKey.four: You counted how often each point is hit. The number of distinct points is 12/4.

explain.text: $4j \bmod 12$ takes the values 0, 4 and 8, so the 12 roots land on 3 points. At $k = 5$ all twelve images differ, since $5j \bmod 12$ hits every residue.

screens.title: When a power is e
screens.prose: The **order** $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ is the least $m \ge 1$ with $g^m = e$ (Pinter writes $\operatorname{ord}(a)$ too). The powers of $g$ form $\langle g \rangle$. A group equal to some $\langle g \rangle$ is **cyclic**, and $g$ is a **generator**. Suppose $\operatorname{ord}(g) = m$.
screens.question: Order the proof that $g^k = e$ exactly when $m \mid k$. Leave out the false line.

lines.text: Write $k = qm + t$ with $0 \le t < m$, by the division algorithm.
If $g^k = e$, then $g^t = e$ with $0 \le t < m$.
$m$ is the least positive power giving $e$, so $t = 0$ and $m \mid k$.

lines.why: You set $k = m$. But $g^{2m} = (g^m)^2 = e$ too, so $k$ can be any multiple of $m$.

hints.text: Divide k by m and keep the remainder.
The remainder $t$ is smaller than $m$, so $g^t = e$ forces $t = 0$.
Divide, simplify, assume, use minimality, then the converse.

feedback.correct: That is the proof, the same division as in Euclid's algorithm.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start with the division of k by m.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step the proof needs.

explain.text: Dividing $k$ by $m$ leaves a remainder $t < m$ with $g^t = g^k$. If that is $e$, minimality forces $t = 0$. So the powers of $g$ that give $e$ are exactly the multiples of $m$.

screens.title: Orders in Z12
screens.prose: In $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ under addition, a power $g^k$ means $g + g + \dots + g$, that is $kg \bmod 12$. Switch the step to see each walk from 0.
screens.question: Fill in the order of each element.

hints.text: Count the steps a walk from 0 takes to return.
8, 16, 24: and 24 is 0 modulo 12.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the element to itself until you reach 0.

screens.title: Generators of Z12
screens.prose: An element generates $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ when its walk from 0 visits all 12 seats, so its order is 12. Try the steps.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which elements generate $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$?

options.why: You chose 3. Its walk is 0, 3, 6, 9: order 4, so it misses most seats.
You chose 9 because it is odd. $\gcd(9, 12) = 3$, so its order is 4.
You chose 2. It reaches only the even seats: order 6.

hints.text: A generator has order 12.
$\operatorname{ord}(k) = 12$ exactly when $\gcd(k, 12) = 1$.
These are the units of l3: 1, 5, 7, 11.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep only the steps whose walk visits every seat.

explain.text: $\operatorname{ord}(k) = 12/\gcd(k, 12)$ is 12 exactly when $\gcd(k, 12) = 1$. So the generators are 1, 5, 7, 11, the four units of l3.

screens.title: The sixth roots of unity
screens.prose: $\mu_6 = \{\zeta^j : j = 0, \dots, 5\}$ with $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/6}$, a turn by $60°$. It is a cyclic group under multiplication, generated by $\zeta$. Here $\zeta^3 = -1$ and $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2) = 3$.
screens.question: Write $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/6}$ as $a + bi$, with $b$ to 3 decimal places.

hints.text: $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ with $\theta = 2\pi/6 = \pi/3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $\cos 60°$ for the real part and $\sin 60°$ for the imaginary part.

byKey.swap: You swapped cosine and sine. The real part is $\cos 60° = 0.5$.

explain.text: $\zeta = \cos 60° + i \sin 60° = 0.5 + 0.866i$. Three turns by $60°$ make $180°$, so $\zeta^3 = -1$. $\zeta^2$ turns by $120°$, so it returns after 3 steps.

screens.title: Not every group is cyclic
screens.prose: $\mathbb{Z}_8^{\times} = \{1, 3, 5, 7\}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_7^{\times} = \{1, \dots, 6\}$ are groups under multiplication. Compare the orders of their elements.
screens.question: Fill in the orders.

hints.text: Multiply the element by itself until you reach 1.
In $\mathbb{Z}_8^{\times}$ the diagonal of the table is all 1s.

feedback.correct: Right. No element of $\mathbb{Z}_8^{\times}$ has order 4, so it is not cyclic. 3 generates $\mathbb{Z}_7^{\times}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply until you reach 1, counting the steps.

explain.text: Every element of $\mathbb{Z}_8^{\times}$ squares to 1, so none generates all four. In $\mathbb{Z}_7^{\times}$, 3 has order 6, so $\mathbb{Z}_7^{\times} = \langle 3 \rangle$ is cyclic.

screens.title: Order of a multiple
screens.prose: In $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, $\operatorname{ord}(1) = 12$, and $8 = 8 \cdot 1$ is the eighth power of 1. A tempting rule says $\operatorname{ord}(g^k) = \operatorname{ord}(g)/k$.
screens.question: What is $\operatorname{ord}(8)$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$?

hints.text: Follow the arrows from 0.
$\operatorname{ord}(8) = 12/\gcd(8, 12) = 12/4 = 3$.

feedback.correct: Right: 3. The rule divides by $\gcd(k, 12)$, not by $k$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Walk from 0 in steps of 8.

byKey.divide: You used $12/8 = 1.5$. An order is a whole number; divide by $\gcd(8, 12) = 4$ instead.
byKey.eight: You gave the element itself. The order is how many steps the walk takes.

explain.text: The walk is $0, 8, 4, 0$: three steps. The true rule is $\operatorname{ord}(g^k) = \operatorname{ord}(g)/\gcd(k, \operatorname{ord}(g))$, here $12/4 = 3$.

screens.title: Futures roll cycles
screens.prose: Months form $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$. Many futures expire quarterly: a desk rolls its position every 3 months, starting in March.
screens.question: How many different months does the roll cycle visit?

hints.text: Follow the arrows from March.
March, June, September, December, then March again.
$\operatorname{ord}(3) = 12/\gcd(3, 12) = 4$.

feedback.correct: Right: March, June, September and December, the quarterly cycle.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Step 3 months at a time from March until you return.

byKey.twelve: You counted every month. Steps of 3 miss the months between.
byKey.three: You gave the step size. Count the months the cycle visits.

explain.text: Steps of 3 visit 4 months because $\operatorname{ord}(3) = 4$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$. A step of 5 months would visit all 12, since 5 generates $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.

screens.title: Two schedules
screens.prose: A fund rebalances every 8 trading days and reviews its risk every 12. Both happen on day 0.
screens.question: After how many trading days do they next fall on the same day?

hints.text: List the multiples of 8 and of 12.
$\operatorname{lcm}(8, 12) = 24$.

feedback.correct: Right: day 24, the least common multiple.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the first day after 0 in both lists.

byKey.product: You multiplied, $8 \times 12 = 96$. They meet sooner, at the least common multiple.
byKey.gcd: You found the gcd, 4. The schedules meet at the lcm.

explain.text: $\operatorname{lcm}(8, 12) = 8 \times 12 / \gcd(8, 12) = 96/4 = 24$. The same lcm gives the order of a pair of cycles in l8.

screens.title: Orders by machine
screens.prose: Write `element_order(g, op, e)`, which applies `op` until it reaches `e`, and `generators(n)` for $\mathbb{Z}_n$ under addition. Stop with `ValueError` after 10,000 steps. Decide what `generators(1)` should be. Passing these cases proves them for these groups only.
screens.question: Finish both functions.

tests.name: mod7
tests.call: element_order(3, lambda a, b: a * b % 7, 1)

tests.name: guard
tests.call: element_order(2, lambda a, b: a * b % 6, 1)

widget.how: The first Check starts Python, which takes a few seconds. Submit runs 8 hidden tests; each must equal the expected value exactly, and the guard case must raise ValueError.

hints.text: Keep a running power x and a counter k.
A generator of Z_n has order n.
$\mathbb{Z}_1 = \{0\}$, and $0$ has order 1 there, so `generators(1)` is `[0]`.

feedback.correct: All eight pass. The guard catches a step that never returns to 1.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Read the first failing row.

explain.text: In $\mathbb{Z}_1 = \{0\}$, the element 0 reaches $e = 0$ at once, so it has order $1 = n$. Modulo 6, 2 cycles through 2 and 4 and never reaches 1, so the guard raises.

ideas: $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ is the least $m \ge 1$ with $g^m = e$, and $g^k = e$ exactly when $m \mid k$.
In $\mathbb{Z}_n$, $\operatorname{ord}(k) = n/\gcd(k, n)$, so the generators are the units.
Not every group is cyclic: every element of $\mathbb{Z}_8^{\times}$ has order at most 2.

quiz.question: A desk rolls every 5 months, starting in January. Which statement is true?

options.text: The cycle visits all 12 months before repeating.

options.why: You took the step as the number of months visited. The order of 5 in Z12 is 12.

options.text: The cycle visits only the odd months.
options.why: You assumed odd steps stay odd. 5 + 5 = 10 is even.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the order of 5 in Z12.

explain.text: $\operatorname{ord}(5) = 12/\gcd(5, 12) = 12$. So every month is visited once before January returns.

options.text: Never: an order is at least 2.

options.why: You mixed order 1 with being a generator. A generator of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ has order 12.

feedback.correct: Right: $g^1 = g$, so $g^1 = e$ means $g = e$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the definition with m = 1.

explain.text: $\operatorname{ord}(g) = 1$ means $g^1 = e$, so $g = e$. Every other element has order at least 2, or infinite order.

options.text: It is cyclic and infinite, generated by 1 and by $-1$.
It is not cyclic, because it is infinite.
options.why: You tied cyclic to finite. Every integer is a multiple of 1, so $\mathbb{Z} = \langle 1 \rangle$.
You chose 2. Its multiples are the even integers, so 1 is missed.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which integers are sums of 1s and −1s?

explain.text: Every integer is $n \cdot 1$, so $\mathbb{Z} = \langle 1 \rangle = \langle -1 \rangle$. No positive multiple of 1 is 0, so 1 has infinite order.

quiz.question: In $\mu_6$, with $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/6}$, what is $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. How many turns by 120° make a full turn?

byKey.six: You gave the order of $\zeta$. $\zeta^2$ turns twice as far each step.
byKey.two: You gave the exponent. Count the powers of ζ² until you reach 1.

explain.text: $\zeta^2$ is a turn by $120°$, so three of them make $360°$. Hence $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2) = 6/\gcd(2, 6) = 3$.
